preamble: An Act to consolidate and amend the provisions relating to offences and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.

glossary.short title: The informal, citable name of an Act — here 'the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023' — fixed by Section 1(1) regardless of the Act's formal number (45 of 2023).
glossary.staggered commencement: A drafting technique (Section 1(3)) where an Act does not come into force on the date the President assents to it, but on a later date the Central Government notifies in the Official Gazette — giving the executive time to prepare rules, infrastructure, and transition from the old law (here, the Indian Penal Code, 1860) before the new one binds anyone.
glossary.extraterritorial jurisdiction: The principle, carried from Section 1(4)-(5) of the BNS (mirroring the old IPC Sections 3-4), that Indian criminal law can reach acts committed outside India's territory if the offender is an Indian citizen, is on an Indian-registered ship or aircraft anywhere, or targets a computer resource located in India — so 'offence under this Sanhita' is not confined to acts physically committed within Indian soil.
glossary.offence targeting a computer resource: A new ground of jurisdiction under Section 1(5)(c) BNS (no IPC equivalent) — any person, of any nationality, anywhere in the world, who commits an offence under the Sanhita that targets a computer resource located in India can be tried as if the offence occurred within India. This was added to address cross-border cybercrime that the IPC's territorial scheme could not reach.
glossary.mutiny and desertion savings clause: Section 1(6), which expressly carves military offences of mutiny and desertion by members of the Army, Navy, or Air Force out of the BNS's reach where they are already governed by the Army Act, 1950, the Navy Act, 1957, or the Air Force Act, 1950 — preventing double jeopardy between the general criminal code and the special military codes.
glossary.dishonestly: Defined in Section 2(10) BNS: doing something with the intention of causing wrongful gain to one person or wrongful loss to another. It is the mental element that separates many property offences (like theft and cheating) from innocent dealings in property — the focus is on transferring entitlement wrongfully, not merely on dishonesty in a lay moral sense.
glossary.fraudulently: Defined in Section 2(12) BNS: a person is said to do a thing fraudulently if they do it with intent to defraud but not otherwise. Courts read this as requiring both deception and an intention to cause actual injury (to person, property, or rights) — deception alone, without that injurious intent, does not satisfy the definition.
glossary.document (BNS definition): Defined in Section 2(9) BNS to mean any matter expressed or described upon any substance by means of letters, figures, or marks, or by more than one of those means, intended to be used or which may be used as evidence of that matter — deliberately medium-neutral so it covers paper writings, electronic records, photographs, and any other durable recording of information capable of evidentiary use.
glossary.public servant (BNS definition): Defined in Section 2(28) BNS through ten lettered sub-clauses (a) to (j) listing categories such as Armed Forces officers, judges, court officers, jurors/assessors, arbitrators, local-authority officers, government-remunerated officers, election officials, and any officer whose duty is to maintain public order or protect the public interest, or who holds office empowering them to exercise government-like functions. The definition is deliberately broad to capture any person performing a public function, regardless of exact appointment mode or pay source.
glossary.offence (BNS definition): Defined in Section 2(25) BNS: an act or omission made punishable by any law for the time being in force, and includes any act in respect of which a complaint may be made under Section 20 of the Cattle-trespass Act, 1871. This cross-referencing definition is what lets the BNS's General Part (definitions, exceptions, abetment, etc.) apply to offences created outside the Sanhita itself, in special and local laws, unless those laws say otherwise.
glossary.voluntarily: Defined in Section 2(38) BNS: a person is said to cause an effect 'voluntarily' when they cause it by means whereby they intended to cause it, or by means which, at the time of employing those means, they knew or had reason to believe to be likely to cause it. This definition anchors offences like voluntarily causing hurt — the actor need not have specifically intended the exact harm, only known it was a likely consequence of the means chosen.
glossary.wrongful gain and wrongful loss: Correlative terms in Section 2(39) BNS: 'wrongful gain' is gain of property by unlawful means to which the person gaining is not legally entitled; 'wrongful loss' is loss of property by unlawful means to which the person losing it is legally entitled. The clause also fixes the doctrinal point that a person can both wrongfully gain and wrongfully lose by keeping property as well as by acquiring it. These definitions anchor 'dishonestly' and the whole scheme of property offences.
glossary.good faith: Defined in Section 2(14) BNS: nothing is said to be done or believed in 'good faith' which is done or believed without due care and attention. This is a demanding, objective standard — mere honest belief is not enough; the person must have exercised the care and attention a reasonable person would, making 'good faith' a frequently litigated gateway to defences and exceptions throughout the Sanhita (e.g. the General Exceptions in Chapter III).
glossary.valuable security: Defined in Section 2(37) BNS: a document which is, or purports to be, a document whereby any legal right is created, extended, transferred, restricted, extinguished, or released, or whereby any person acknowledges that they lie under a legal liability or have not a certain legal right. Forgery, cheating, and extortion offences frequently turn on whether the instrument obtained or altered qualifies as a 'valuable security' in this technical sense.
glossary.child (BNS definition): Defined in Section 2(7) BNS to mean any person below the age of eighteen years — a single, Sanhita-wide definition that feeds into aggravating provisions throughout the Act (e.g. offences against children, kidnapping, trafficking) wherever the text uses the word 'child' rather than 'minor' or a specific numeric age threshold of its own.
glossary.General Exceptions overlay: The effect of Section 3(1) BNS, which provides that the General Exceptions contained in Chapter III (e.g. mistake of fact, accident, necessity, consent, private defence) apply to every provision of the Sanhita in the same manner as if each exception were repeated within the text of every defining section — so a defendant can always invoke Chapter III even though an individual offence-defining section never mentions it.
glossary.constructive possession: The concept, embedded in Section 3(5)-(6) BNS, that a person is deemed to be 'in possession' of movable property not only when they hold it directly but also when it is in the possession of another person who holds it subject to that person's control, or who holds it on that person's behalf — relevant to theft, criminal misappropriation, and similar property offences where physical custody and legal possession diverge.
glossary.acts extending to illegal omissions: A drafting rule in Section 3(2) BNS: wherever the Sanhita uses a word that denotes an act done, that word (unless a contrary intention appears) also covers an illegal omission to act — so offences framed in terms of 'doing' something can, in appropriate cases, be committed by unlawfully failing to act where there was a legal duty to act.
glossary.common intention: The principle under Section 3(8) BNS (the BNS's version of the former IPC Section 34) that when a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of their common intention, each of them is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by them alone — a constructive-joint-liability doctrine requiring a shared pre-arranged plan or meeting of minds, illustrated in the Sanhita by the three-person beating example.
glossary.common criminal knowledge or intention: The principle under Section 3(9) BNS (the BNS's version of the former IPC Section 35): whenever an act is criminal only because of the criminal intention or knowledge of the person doing it, several persons who join in that act are liable only to the extent of their own individual criminal intention or knowledge — so joint participants can incur different degrees of liability for the same physical act, unlike the equal liability imposed under 'common intention.'
glossary.cooperation in several acts constituting: Section 3(7) BNS: when an offence is committed by means of several acts, whoever intentionally cooperates in the commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, commits that offence — covering division-of-labour scenarios where no single participant performs every act that makes up the offence.
glossary.differential liability among co-particip: The outcome illustrated under Section 3(9) BNS: where criminal liability turns on each individual's own knowledge or intention rather than a shared common intention, co-participants in the same physical act can be convicted of offences of different gravity — e.g. one participant convicted of murder while another, lacking the requisite knowledge or intention, is convicted only of a lesser offence for the very same incident.

sections.title: Short title, commencement and application
sections.raw_text:
(1) This Act may be called the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
(2) It shall come into force on such date as the Central Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, appoint, and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of this Sanhita.
(3) Every person shall be liable to punishment under this Sanhita and not otherwise for every act or omission contrary to the provisions thereof, of which he shall be guilty within India.
(4) Any person liable, by any law for the time being in force in India, to be tried for an offence committed beyond India shall be dealt with according to the provisions of this Sanhita for any act committed beyond India in the same manner as if such act had been committed within India.
(5) The provisions of this Sanhita shall also apply to any offence committed by—
(a) any citizen of India in any place without and beyond India;
(b) any person on any ship or aircraft registered in India wherever it may be;
(c) any person in any place without and beyond India committing offence targeting a computer resource located in India.
Explanation.—In this section, the word “offence” includes every act committed outside India which, if committed in India, would be punishable under this Sanhita.
Illustration.—A, who is a citizen of India, commits a murder in any place without and beyond India. He can be tried and convicted of murder in any place in India in which he may be found.
(6) Nothing in this Sanhita shall affect the provisions of any Act for punishing mutiny and desertion of officers, soldiers, sailors or airmen in the service of the Government of India or the provisions of any special or local law.

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 1 is the Sanhita's opening gateway clause: it names the Act, hands the Central Government a notification-based switch to bring different provisions into force on different dates rather than all at once, lays down the basic rule that criminal liability in India flows only from this Sanhita (not any residual common-law notion of crime), and then extends that liability outward to Indian citizens abroad, to anyone on an Indian-registered ship or aircraft anywhere in the world, and — reflecting a problem the 1860 Penal Code never had to address — to anyone sitting outside India who targets a computer resource located inside India. A closing savings clause keeps military mutiny/desertion law and other special or local laws untouched.
essential_elements: Clause (1): fixes the short title as 'the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023'
Clause (2): staggered-commencement power — the Central Government may notify different dates for different provisions, not necessarily one single commencement date for the whole Sanhita
Clause (3): the core territorial principle — liability for acts/omissions within India arises under this Sanhita 'and not otherwise'
Clause (4): extraterritorial offences are tried exactly as if committed within India

Clause (5): three specific extraterritorial hooks — (a) Indian citizens anywhere abroad, (b) anyone on an Indian-registered ship or aircraft, (c) anyone abroad who targets a computer resource located in India
Clause (6): preserves military mutiny/desertion legislation and other special or local laws from being displaced by this Sanhita's general scheme
exceptions_and_qualifications: The extraterritorial clause (5)(c) targeting a computer resource located in India is a new addition with no equivalent in the old Indian Penal Code, 1860 — it is the hook used to prosecute cross-border cyber-offences

Clause (6) is a savings/non-obstante-style carve-out, not a substantive exception to who is liable — it only confirms this Sanhita does not override military discipline law or other special/local statutes

Because commencement can be staggered under clause (2), different BNS sections can theoretically take effect on different notified dates even though the Sanhita as a whole was brought into force in a single notification
breakdown.how_to_read: Read clause (5) as the extraterritorial reach provision — in practice its sub-clause (c) is the one practitioners cite for cross-border cyber-crime jurisdiction. Clause (6) should never be read as narrowing the Sanhita's own scope; it is purely a non-displacement clause protecting other statutes.

sections.title: Definitions

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 2 is the Sanhita's master glossary — 39 numbered clauses defining the vocabulary every later offence-definition relies on. Most carry forward almost word-for-word from the old Indian Penal Code's Section 8 to Section 52A (dishonestly, fraudulently, document, voluntarily, public servant, valuable security, and so on), so decades of IPC case law construing these exact phrases remains directly relevant. A few are updated or new: 'document' now expressly includes electronic and digital records, 'gender' is defined by cross-reference to the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019, and clause (39) imports any term the Sanhita itself leaves undefined from the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (the companion criminal-procedure code).
essential_elements: Clauses (1)-(39) each define a single term or term-pair used throughout the Sanhita's substantive offence provisions
Clause (8) 'document' is explicitly widened beyond paper to include electronic and digital records — a change from the undiluted IPC-era definition

Clause (24) 'offence' has a split meaning: the default sense (punishable only under this Sanhita) is overridden for an enumerated list of sections, where 'offence' instead reaches conduct punishable under any special or local law too

Clause (28) 'public servant' is an exhaustive ten-category list (commissioned officers, Judges, Court officers, panchayat members, arbitrators, confinement-empowered officers, law-enforcement officers, revenue/pecuniary officers, local-rights officers, election officials, and government-service personnel) plus two deeming Explanations
Clause (39) is a residual cross-reference clause pulling in undefined terms from the Information Technology Act, 2000 and the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (24)'s 'offence' definition is itself subject to two carve-outs (sub-clauses (a) and (b)) listing dozens of specific sections where the narrower IPC-style meaning does not apply — always check whether the section you are working with appears on either list before assuming the default definition governs

Clause (28)(k)(ii)'s 'public servant' extension to local-authority and government-company employees depends on cross-referenced definitions in the General Clauses Act, 1897 and the Companies Act, 2013, so confirming public-servant status for such an employee requires checking those external definitions too

Because most definitions reproduce IPC wording verbatim, pre-2024 Supreme Court and High Court judgments interpreting the identical IPC phrase remain persuasive (often binding) authority for the BNS equivalent
breakdown.how_to_read: Use this section as a lookup table, not a provision to memorise wholesale — when an offence section uses a defined term in quotation marks, cross-check its exact clause here first, since several terms (especially 'offence', 'document', and 'public servant') carry carve-outs or extensions that change the outcome of a case.

sections.title: General explanations
sections.raw_text:
(1) Throughout this Sanhita every definition of an offence, every penal provision, and every Illustration of every such definition or penal provision, shall be understood subject to the exceptions contained in the Chapter entitled “General Exceptions”, though those exceptions are not repeated in such definition, penal provision, or Illustration.
Illustrations.—(a) The sections in this Sanhita, which contain definitions of offences, do not express that a child under seven years of age cannot commit such offences; but the definitions are to be understood subject to the general exception which provides that nothing shall be an offence which is done by a child under seven years of age. (b) A, a police officer, without warrant, apprehends Z, who has committed murder. Here A is not guilty of the offence of wrongful confinement; for he was bound by law to apprehend Z, and therefore the case falls within the general exception which provides that “nothing is an offence which is done by a person who is bound by law to do it”.
(2) Every expression which is explained in any Part of this Sanhita, is used in every Part of this Sanhita in conformity with the explanation.
(3) When property is in the possession of a person’s spouse, clerk or servant, on account of that person, it is in that person’s possession within the meaning of this Sanhita. Explanation.—A person employed temporarily or on a particular occasion in the capacity of a clerk or servant, is a clerk or servant within the meaning of this sub-section.
(4) In every Part of this Sanhita, except where a contrary intention appears from the context, words which refer to acts done extend also to illegal omissions.
(5) When a criminal act is done by several persons in furtherance of the common intention of all, each of such persons is liable for that act in the same manner as if it were done by him alone.
(6) Whenever an act, which is criminal only by reason of its being done with a criminal knowledge or intention, is done by several persons, each of such persons who joins in the act with such knowledge or intention is liable for the act in the same manner as if the act were done by him alone with that knowledge or intention.
(7) Wherever the causing of a certain effect, or an attempt to cause that effect, by an act or by an omission, is an offence, it is to be understood that the causing of that effect partly by an act and partly by an omission is the same offence.
Illustration.—A intentionally causes Z’s death, partly by illegally omitting to give Z food, and partly by beating Z. A has committed murder.
(8) When an offence is committed by means of several acts, whoever intentionally cooperates in the commission of that offence by doing any one of those acts, either singly or jointly with any other person, commits that offence.
Illustrations.—(a) A and B agree to murder Z by severally and at different times giving him small doses of poison. A and B administer the poison according to the agreement with intent to murder Z. Z dies from the effects the several doses of poison so administered to him. Here A and B intentionally cooperate in the commission of murder and as each of them does an act by which the death is caused, they are both guilty of the offence though their acts are separate. (b) A and B are joint jailors, and as such have the charge of Z, a prisoner, alternatively for six hours at a time. A and B, intending to cause Z’s death, knowingly cooperate in causing that effect by illegally omitting, each during the time of his attendance, to furnish Z with food supplied to them for that purpose. Z dies of hunger. Both A and B are guilty of the murder of Z. (c) A, a jailor, has the charge of Z, a prisoner. A, intending to cause Z’s death, illegally omits to supply Z with food; in consequence of which Z is much reduced in strength, but the starvation is not sufficient to cause his death. A is dismissed from his office, and B succeeds him. B, without collusion or cooperation with A, illegally omits to supply Z with food, knowing that he is likely thereby to cause Z’s death. Z dies of hunger. B is guilty of murder, but, as A did not cooperate with B, A is guilty only of an attempt to commit murder.
(9) Where several persons are engaged or concerned in the commission of a criminal act, they may be guilty of different offences by means of that act.
Illustration.—A attacks Z under such circumstances of grave provocation that his killing of Z would be only culpable homicide not amounting to murder. B, having ill-will towards Z and intending to kill him, and not having been subject to the provocation, assists A in killing Z. Here, though A and B are both engaged in causing Z’s death, B is guilty of murder, and A is guilty only of culpable homicide.
key_terms: cooperation in several acts constituting one offence

breakdown.plain_summary: Section 3 lays down nine interpretive ground rules that apply across the entire Sanhita rather than to any single offence. The most important is clause (1): every offence-definition is automatically read subject to Chapter III's General Exceptions even though those exceptions are never repeated section by section — so, for example, the fact that a seven-year-old cannot be convicted of murder is never stated in the murder section itself, only in the General Exceptions chapter. The remaining clauses fix constructive-possession rules, extend act-based language to cover illegal omissions, and — most consequentially for group crime — establish that persons acting with a common intention, a shared criminal knowledge/intention, or merely cooperating through separate acts in the same offence are each liable as if they alone had committed the whole offence; yet clause (9)'s illustration shows participants in the same criminal episode can still end up convicted of genuinely different offences depending on their individual mental state.
essential_elements: Clause (1): every offence definition, penal provision, and illustration is automatically subject to Chapter III's General Exceptions, even without express repetition
Clause (2): a term explained anywhere in the Sanhita carries that same meaning everywhere else in the Sanhita
Clause (3): property held by a person's spouse, clerk, or servant on that person's account counts as being in that person's own possession
Clause (4): references to 'acts' extend to illegal omissions unless a contrary intention appears
Clause (5): common-intention liability — each participant in a group act done in furtherance of the common intention of all is liable as if he alone did the whole act
Clause (6): common-knowledge-or-intention liability for acts that are criminal only because of the knowledge/intention behind them
Clause (7): causing an effect partly by act and partly by omission is treated as the same offence as causing it wholly by act or wholly by omission
Clause (8): cooperating in any one of several acts that together constitute an offence makes a person guilty of that offence
Clause (9): several persons engaged in one criminal act or transaction may nonetheless be convicted of different offences from each other, depending on individual intent or circumstance
exceptions_and_qualifications: Clause (1) is an interpretive default, not an independent defence — a defendant must still actually satisfy the elements of a specific General Exception (e.g. the age, unsoundness-of-mind, or compulsion provisions in Chapter III) for it to apply

Clause (3)'s constructive-possession rule only reaches spouse/clerk/servant relationships 'on account of' the person — mere physical custody by an unrelated third party does not automatically transfer possession

Clause (9) is the key qualification on clauses (5)-(8): shared participation in one transaction does not force identical liability on every participant — grave provocation, lack of prior common intention, or absence of the requisite knowledge can produce different convictions (e.g. murder for one, culpable homicide not amounting to murder for another) out of the same episode
breakdown.how_to_read: Treat clauses (5) and (6) as the Sanhita's general group-liability engine (the BNS's equivalent of the old IPC's 'common intention' and 'common object' architecture) — but always test clause (9) against the facts before assuming every co-accused shares the same offence; grave and sudden provocation or absence of common intention is exactly what can split liability within the same group act, as its own illustration demonstrates.
